title: Sh-U-V
hookLine: teshuvah, from the root to turn or return

cards: Three widows stand on a road leading out of Moab. Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she tells her two daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' houses. "Turn again, my daughters," she says.
Orpah kisses her and turns back. Ruth won't; she goes on with Naomi. Then the chapter ends with a strange line: Naomi returned, and Ruth with her, "which returned out of the country of Moab."
Ruth returned. To a place she had never been. The verb doing all that turning and returning is today's root.

teach.h: RUTH RETURNS TO A NEW PLACE.
teach.b: Sh-U-V. Shin, vav, vet. To turn, to return.
From it comes teshuvah, the word often translated repentance; way back on day nineteen, you met it as return. Turn it four ways. First, Ruth.
Her first chapter keeps coming back to this verb, and it lets Ruth return to a land she's never seen. So teshuvah isn't only going back to where you were. It can be turning toward where you belong.
Second, the prophet's call. Hosea says: "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God."
That verse is read on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and that Sabbath takes its name from it: Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath of Return. Third, both directions.

teach.h: TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.
teach.b: Lamentations ends with a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Turn us, and we'll turn: asked for and done at the same time.
Those words are sung in synagogue as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark. Fourth, how you know it's real.
Maimonides, in his Laws of Teshuvah, says complete teshuvah is when the same situation comes around again, with the same pull, and the person, able to do the same thing, chooses differently.
Not because the door is locked. Because they've turned. Not a feeling of regret, but a change of direction you can see.

how: Teshuvah is a theme of the season from the month of Elul through Yom Kippur, and a blessing asking for return is also part of the weekday Amidah prayer.

o: to wander off and lose your way
to turn or return; the root of teshuvah
to feel deep regret for something done

games.q: the root of turning — tap the pairs.
p: turned back to her mother's house
returned to a place she'd never been
named for Hosea's call to return

s: teshuvah only means going back to where you were
Ruth 'returned' to a land she had never seen. the root also means turning toward.
the words 'turn thou us unto thee' are sung as the Torah returns to the ark
they come from the end of Lamentations.
for Maimonides, regret is enough for complete teshuvah
he looks for the same situation, the same pull, and a different choice.

games.q: a year after you made a promise to change, the same situation comes back, with the same pull. you could do it again. what does Maimonides call complete teshuvah?
o: staying far away so it can't happen.
being able to do it, and choosing differently.
games.why: in his Laws of Teshuvah, complete return is when the same chance comes and the person turns from it, not because they can't, but because they've changed.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you've drifted from: a call you keep not making, a habit that slipped, a person you've been short with.

Don't build a case against yourself; just find the direction you've been facing and the one you'd rather face, and in your mind, make the turn. If you pray, you can say the words from Lamentations: turn us, and we shall be turned.

wordCard.voice: Sh-U-V. Shin, vav, vet: to turn, to return. The root of teshuvah, the turning a person can choose. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, repentance; from the root shin, vav, vet, to turn.

carryVoice: Your line: turn. Teshuvah is a direction you can see, not only a feeling. Rest well.
